newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arianespace delays picking boss after French vote.
newsitem.headline: Arianespace delays picking boss after French vote.

text.p: Europe's Arianespace rocket launch firm delayed naming a new president on Monday as France's new Socialist-led government added a twist to a bitter power struggle.

The favourite for the job before Prime Minister Lionel Jospin came to power two weeks ago was Jean-Marie Luton, head of the European Space Agency (ESA) since 1990 and who was seen by many Arianespace officials as too close to the ousted centre-right coalition.
"The recently formed French government has asked to be briefed on all important decisions to be taken in all areas," the company said in a statement at the Paris airshow.
Arianespace is controlled by French government-owned companies and organisations that hold a 55-percent share in the company. The French Space Agency (CNES) alone holds 32 percent.
German companies hold 18 percent and Italy eight percent. The rest is held by companies is nine other countries mostly in the European Union.

"Under these conditions, the annual general meeting decided to defer its ruling on the proposed resolutions and therefore, to adjourn the session," Arianespace said. A new meeting is slated for June 30.

The annual shareholders meeting had been expected to confirm the appointment of Luton as Arianespace's new chairman despite opposition from Charles Bigot, the company's president who is scheduled to retire on July 1.

Sources close to Arianespace management said Bigot was furious the former government in April virtually eliminated his deputy and favoured successor at Arianespace, Francis Avanzi, in favour of Luton.

Bigot recruited Avanzi, who has held the number two spot at the company since 1995. Avanzi was formally chairman of aircraft engine maker CFM International and has a reputation as an aggressive salesman and a strong leader.
"Bigot is completely disgusted and is not at the airshow. He is fed up with the turn of events," they said. The company also cancelled an annual press conference until June 30.
Industry analysts were uncertain whether Jospin's government would back Luton. Company officials had criticised him as someone who would merely follow instructions from the former government.

Arianespace has led the commercial satellite launch market since the mid 1980s but has recently come under pressure from U.S. consolidation, notably the creation of Lockheed Martin and the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas by Boeing.
